title: What it means for a machine to "learn": fitting a function to data
summary: A model is a function with knobs. A loss measures how wrong it is on known examples, and learning means nudging the knobs until the loss stops falling. The test of learning is a sensible answer for an input the model has never seen.
llm_link: A language model is a function from the text so far to a guess about the next token. Instead of two knobs it has billions of parameters, and training is the same loop: measure the loss on real text, nudge every parameter to lower it, repeat.
key_ideas: A function takes an input and returns exactly one output. A model is a function with adjustable numbers (parameters, or knobs).
A straight line price = m · size + b has two knobs: the slope m and the height b where it crosses the vertical axis.
The loss (here the mean squared error) averages the squared gaps between predictions and true values. Squaring makes misses above and below both count.
Learning = start the knobs anywhere, nudge them in whichever direction lowers the loss, repeat until no nudge helps.
A model has learned when it gives sensible outputs for inputs it never saw, not when it memorises the examples.

quiz.q: In this lesson, what does it mean for a machine to "learn"?
options: It stores every example so it can look them up later
It adjusts its parameters so that its loss on the examples goes down
A programmer writes the exact rule into the code
It picks the line that passes through the first two points
quiz.explain: Nobody types the final rule. The knobs start anywhere and are nudged in the direction that lowers the loss, so the rule is found by search.

quiz.q: Predict the result: the line is guess = 2 · x + 1. The data is (x=1, y=4) and (x=2, y=5). What is the mean squared error?
quiz.explain: Guesses are 3 and 5. Gaps are 3 − 4 = −1 and 5 − 5 = 0. Squared: 1 and 0. The average of 1 and 0 is 0.5.

quiz.q: Why do we square each gap before averaging?
options: So that a miss above and a miss below cannot cancel each other out
Squaring is optional and changes nothing
quiz.explain: Without squaring, a gap of +3 and a gap of −3 would average to 0, and a terrible line would look perfect. Squares are never negative, so every miss counts against the line (and big misses count a lot).

quiz.q: Two models have the same loss on the flats they were trained on. Which one has learned better?
options: The one that gives more sensible prices for flats that were not in the record
The one that was trained for longer
They are equally good by definition
quiz.explain: Fitting the old examples is the means, not the goal. What we care about is the next input, so we judge a model on data it has not seen.

quiz.q: In a large language model, what plays the role of the slope and height knobs?
options: Billions of numeric parameters (weights) that training nudges to lower the loss
A list of rules written by engineers
quiz.explain: The prompt is the input, like the size of the flat. The weights are the knobs, and training nudges them to lower the loss on predicting the next token.

problems.title: Predict and measure the loss
problems.prompt:
A line is described by two knobs, m (slope) and b (height). Write:

  • predict(m, b, x): the line's guess for input x.
  • mse(m, b, xs, ys): the mean squared error of the line on the data, i.e. the average over all points of (guess − true value)².
predict(2, 1, 3)                 # 7
mse(2, 1, [1, 2], [4, 5])        # 0.5

xs and ys are plain Python lists of the same length; ys[i] is the true value for xs[i].

tests.name: predict on a simple line
tests.code:
out = predict(2, 1, 3)
assert out == 7, f'predict(2, 1, 3) should be 2*3 + 1 = 7, got {out}'

tests.name: predict with a negative slope
tests.code:
out = predict(-0.5, 4, 2)
assert abs(out - 3) < 1e-9, f'predict(-0.5, 4, 2) should be -0.5*2 + 4 = 3, got {out}'

tests.name: mse of the quiz example
tests.code:
out = mse(2, 1, [1, 2], [4, 5])
assert out is not None, 'mse returned None; did you forget to return the result?'
assert abs(out - 0.5) < 1e-9, f'guesses are 3 and 5, gaps -1 and 0, squares 1 and 0, average 0.5; got {out}'

tests.name: a perfect line has zero loss
tests.code:
out = mse(3, -1, [0, 1, 2, 5], [-1, 2, 5, 14])
assert abs(out) < 1e-9, f'every point lies on y = 3x - 1, so the loss should be 0, got {out}'

tests.name: misses above and below do not cancel
tests.code:
out = mse(0, 0, [1, 2], [3, -3])
assert abs(out - 9) < 1e-9, f'gaps are -3 and +3; squared they are 9 and 9, average 9. Got {out}. If you got 0, you forgot to square.'

tests.name: it is an average, not a sum
tests.code:
out = mse(0, 0, [1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 1, 1, 1])
assert abs(out - 1) < 1e-9, f'four gaps of 1 should average to 1, got {out}. Did you divide by len(xs)?'

hints: predict is one line: return m * x + b
Walk both lists together: for x, y in zip(xs, ys): gap = predict(m, b, x) - y
Add gap ** 2 to total inside the loop, then return total / len(xs) after it.

problems.title: Learn by nudging the knobs
problems.prompt:
Now make the machine learn, exactly as in the video: try a small nudge to each knob and keep whichever setting lowers the loss.

Write nudge(m, b, xs, ys, step). Consider the five settings (m, b), (m+step, b), (m-step, b), (m, b+step), (m, b-step) and return the one with the lowest mse as a tuple (m, b). If no nudge helps, the current setting wins.

Then write fit(xs, ys, steps, step) that starts at m = 0, b = 0, calls nudge steps times and returns the final (m, b).

predict and mse from the previous problem are already included.

tests.name: nudge moves towards the data
tests.code:
m, b = nudge(0, 0, [1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], 0.5)
assert (m, b) == (0.5, 0), f'from (0, 0) the best single nudge for y = 2x is m + 0.5, giving (0.5, 0); got {(m, b)}'

tests.name: nudge stays put when nothing helps
tests.code:
m, b = nudge(2, 0, [1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], 0.1)
assert (m, b) == (2, 0), f'(2, 0) already fits y = 2x perfectly, so every nudge makes the loss worse; got {(m, b)}'

tests.name: nudge returns a tuple
tests.code:
out = nudge(0, 0, [1], [1], 0.1)
assert isinstance(out, tuple) and len(out) == 2, f'nudge should return a tuple (m, b), got {out!r}'

tests.name: fit lowers the loss a lot
tests.code:
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; ys = [3.1, 4.9, 7.2, 8.8, 11.1]
m, b = fit(xs, ys, 400, 0.05)
assert mse(m, b, xs, ys) < 0.1, f'after 400 nudges the loss should be under 0.1 (start was {mse(0, 0, xs, ys):.1f}); got {mse(m, b, xs, ys):.3f} with m={m:.2f}, b={b:.2f}. Is fit calling nudge in a loop and keeping its result?'

tests.name: fit finds the trend
tests.code:
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; ys = [3.1, 4.9, 7.2, 8.8, 11.1]
m, b = fit(xs, ys, 400, 0.05)
assert abs(m - 2) < 0.3 and abs(b - 1) < 0.6, f'the data roughly follows y = 2x + 1; got m={m:.2f}, b={b:.2f}'

hints: Keep the best candidate seen so far: best = candidates[0], then loop and replace best whenever mse(*c, xs, ys) < mse(*best, xs, ys).
Python can do it in one line: min(candidates, key=lambda c: mse(c[0], c[1], xs, ys))
In fit: for _ in range(steps): m, b = nudge(m, b, xs, ys, step)
